question.:question/problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral of the function $f(x,y,z)=\frac{y+z}{x},$ traversed along the line segment from $(-5,-3,5)$ to $(-4,-5,7)?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For scalar arc length, use

$$
\int_C f\,\mathrm{d}s=\int_0^1 f(\mathbf r(t))\|\mathbf r^{\prime}(t)\|\,\mathrm{d}t
$$

Parametrize the segment and check its endpoints:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r(t)&=A+t(B-A) \\  &=\left(t - 5,- 2 t - 3,2 t + 5\right) \\  \mathbf r(0)&=\left(-5,-3,5\right) \\  \mathbf r(1)&=\left(-4,-5,7\right)\end{aligned}
$$

For $0\le t\le1$, the velocity and speed are

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r^{\prime}(t)&=\left(1,-2,2\right) \\  \|\mathbf r^{\prime}(t)\|&=\sqrt{(1)^2+(-2)^2+(2)^2} \\  &=3\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute all three coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf r(t))&=\frac{(- 2 t - 3)+(2 t + 5)}{t - 5} \\  &=\frac{2}{t - 5}\end{aligned}
$$

The equivalent definite integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C f\,\mathrm{d}s&=3{\int }_{0}^{1}\left(\frac{2}{t - 5}\right)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral of the function $f(x,y,z)=\sqrt{2x+y-z},$ traversed along the line segment from $(1,1,1)$ to $(3,-1,0)?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For scalar arc length, use

$$
\int_C f\,\mathrm{d}s=\int_0^1 f(\mathbf r(t))\|\mathbf r^{\prime}(t)\|\,\mathrm{d}t
$$

Parametrize the segment and check its endpoints:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r(t)&=A+t(B-A) \\  &=\left(2 t + 1,1 - 2 t,1 - t\right) \\  \mathbf r(0)&=\left(1,1,1\right) \\  \mathbf r(1)&=\left(3,-1,0\right)\end{aligned}
$$

For $0\le t\le1$, the velocity and speed are

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r^{\prime}(t)&=\left(2,-2,-1\right) \\  \|\mathbf r^{\prime}(t)\|&=\sqrt{(2)^2+(-2)^2+(-1)^2} \\  &=3\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute all three coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf r(t))&=\sqrt{2(2 t + 1)+(1 - 2 t)-(1 - t)} \\  &=\sqrt{3 t + 2}\end{aligned}
$$

The equivalent definite integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C f\,\mathrm{d}s&=3{\int }_{0}^{1}(\sqrt{3 t + 2})\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral of the function $f(x, y, z) = x + y + z$, traversed along the line segment from $(-1, 1, -4)$ to $(0, 4, -7)$?
question.:question/worked-solution:
For scalar arc length, use

$$
\int_C f\,\mathrm{d}s=\int_0^1 f(\mathbf r(t))\|\mathbf r^{\prime}(t)\|\,\mathrm{d}t
$$

Parametrize the segment and check its endpoints:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r(t)&=A+t(B-A) \\  &=\left(t - 1,3 t + 1,- 3 t - 4\right) \\  \mathbf r(0)&=\left(-1,1,-4\right) \\  \mathbf r(1)&=\left(0,4,-7\right)\end{aligned}
$$

For $0\le t\le1$, the velocity and speed are

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r^{\prime}(t)&=\left(1,3,-3\right) \\  \|\mathbf r^{\prime}(t)\|&=\sqrt{(1)^2+(3)^2+(-3)^2} \\  &=\sqrt{19}\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute all three coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf r(t))&=(t - 1)+(3 t + 1)+(- 3 t - 4) \\  &=t - 4\end{aligned}
$$

The equivalent definite integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C f\,\mathrm{d}s&=\sqrt{19}{\int }_{0}^{1}(t - 4)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{C}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}(x+z))\,\text{d}s$ along the line segment from $(0,4,-3)$ to $(-3,2,-5).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For scalar arc length, use

$$
\int_C f\,\mathrm{d}s=\int_0^1 f(\mathbf r(t))\|\mathbf r^{\prime}(t)\|\,\mathrm{d}t
$$

Parametrize the segment and check its endpoints:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r(t)&=A+t(B-A) \\  &=\left(- 3 t,4 - 2 t,- 2 t - 3\right) \\  \mathbf r(0)&=\left(0,4,-3\right) \\  \mathbf r(1)&=\left(-3,2,-5\right)\end{aligned}
$$

For $0\le t\le1$, the velocity and speed are

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r^{\prime}(t)&=\left(-3,-2,-2\right) \\  \|\mathbf r^{\prime}(t)\|&=\sqrt{(-3)^2+(-2)^2+(-2)^2} \\  &=\sqrt{17}\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute all three coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf r(t))&=\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{4}((- 3 t)+(- 2 t - 3))\right) \\  &=\cos{\left(- \frac{5 \pi t}{4} - \frac{3 \pi}{4} \right)}\end{aligned}
$$

The equivalent definite integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C f\,\mathrm{d}s&=\sqrt{17}{\int }_{0}^{1}(\cos{\left(- \frac{5 \pi t}{4} - \frac{3 \pi}{4} \right)})\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Use $u=- \frac{5 \pi t}{4} - \frac{3 \pi}{4}$ and $\mathrm{d}u=\left(- \frac{5 \pi}{4}\right)\,\mathrm{d}t$. The new bounds are $u(0)=- \frac{3 \pi}{4}$ and $u(1)=- 2 \pi$.

$$
\begin{aligned}I&=- \frac{4 \sqrt{17}}{5 \pi}\int_{- \frac{3 \pi}{4}}^{- 2 \pi}\cos u\,\mathrm{d}u \\  &=- \frac{4 \sqrt{17}}{5 \pi}\left[\sin u\right]_{- \frac{3 \pi}{4}}^{- 2 \pi} \\  &=- \frac{4 \sqrt{17}}{5 \pi}\left(\sin(- 2 \pi)-\sin\left(- \frac{3 \pi}{4}\right)\right) \\  &=- \frac{4 \sqrt{17}}{5 \pi}\left((0)-\left(- \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)\right) \\  &=- \frac{2 \sqrt{34}}{5 \pi}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{C}x{e}^{yz}\,\text{d}s$ along the line segment from $(4,3,1)$ to $(2,2,0).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For scalar arc length, use

$$
\int_C f\,\mathrm{d}s=\int_0^1 f(\mathbf r(t))\|\mathbf r^{\prime}(t)\|\,\mathrm{d}t
$$

Parametrize the segment and check its endpoints:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r(t)&=A+t(B-A) \\  &=\left(4 - 2 t,3 - t,1 - t\right) \\  \mathbf r(0)&=\left(4,3,1\right) \\  \mathbf r(1)&=\left(2,2,0\right)\end{aligned}
$$

For $0\le t\le1$, the velocity and speed are

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r^{\prime}(t)&=\left(-2,-1,-1\right) \\  \|\mathbf r^{\prime}(t)\|&=\sqrt{(-2)^2+(-1)^2+(-1)^2} \\  &=\sqrt{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute all three coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf r(t))&=(4 - 2 t)e^{(3 - t)(1 - t)} \\  &=\left(4 - 2 t\right) e^{t^{2} - 4 t + 3}\end{aligned}
$$

The equivalent definite integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C f\,\mathrm{d}s&=\sqrt{6}{\int }_{0}^{1}(\left(4 - 2 t\right) e^{t^{2} - 4 t + 3})\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Use $u=t^{2} - 4 t + 3$ and $\mathrm{d}u=(2 t - 4)\,\mathrm{d}t$. The new bounds are $u(0)=3$ and $u(1)=0$. Since $x(t)=-1\,u^{\prime}(t)$, the differential contributes the factor $-1$.

$$
\begin{aligned}I&=- \sqrt{6}\int_{3}^{0}e^u\,\mathrm{d}u \\  &=- \sqrt{6}\left[e^u\right]_{3}^{0} \\  &=- \sqrt{6}\left(e^{0}-e^{3}\right) \\  &=- \sqrt{6}\left(1-(e^{3})\right) \\  &=- \sqrt{6} \left(1 - e^{3}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{C}\sin \left(\frac{πy}{4}\right)ds$ along the line segment from $(-1, 1, -4)$ to $(0, 4, -7)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
For scalar arc length, use

$$
\int_C f\,\mathrm{d}s=\int_0^1 f(\mathbf r(t))\|\mathbf r^{\prime}(t)\|\,\mathrm{d}t
$$

Parametrize the segment and check its endpoints:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r(t)&=A+t(B-A) \\  &=\left(t - 1,3 t + 1,- 3 t - 4\right) \\  \mathbf r(0)&=\left(-1,1,-4\right) \\  \mathbf r(1)&=\left(0,4,-7\right)\end{aligned}
$$

For $0\le t\le1$, the velocity and speed are

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r^{\prime}(t)&=\left(1,3,-3\right) \\  \|\mathbf r^{\prime}(t)\|&=\sqrt{(1)^2+(3)^2+(-3)^2} \\  &=\sqrt{19}\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute all three coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf r(t))&=\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{4}(3 t + 1)\right) \\  &=\sin{\left(\frac{3 \pi t}{4} + \frac{\pi}{4} \right)}\end{aligned}
$$

The equivalent definite integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C f\,\mathrm{d}s&=\sqrt{19}{\int }_{0}^{1}(\sin{\left(\frac{3 \pi t}{4} + \frac{\pi}{4} \right)})\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Use $u=\frac{3 \pi t}{4} + \frac{\pi}{4}$ and $\mathrm{d}u=\left(\frac{3 \pi}{4}\right)\,\mathrm{d}t$. The new bounds are $u(0)=\frac{\pi}{4}$ and $u(1)=\pi$.

$$
\begin{aligned}I&=\frac{4 \sqrt{19}}{3 \pi}\int_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\pi}\sin u\,\mathrm{d}u \\  &=\frac{4 \sqrt{19}}{3 \pi}\left[-\cos u\right]_{\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\pi} \\  &=\frac{4 \sqrt{19}}{3 \pi}\left(-\cos(\pi)+\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\right) \\  &=\frac{4 \sqrt{19}}{3 \pi}\left((1)-\left(- \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)\right) \\  &=\frac{2 \sqrt{19} \left(\sqrt{2} + 2\right)}{3 \pi}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{C}x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}s$ along the line segment from $(3,1,1)$ to $(1,4,4).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For scalar arc length, use

$$
\int_C f\,\mathrm{d}s=\int_0^1 f(\mathbf r(t))\|\mathbf r^{\prime}(t)\|\,\mathrm{d}t
$$

Parametrize the segment and check its endpoints:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r(t)&=A+t(B-A) \\  &=\left(3 - 2 t,3 t + 1,3 t + 1\right) \\  \mathbf r(0)&=\left(3,1,1\right) \\  \mathbf r(1)&=\left(1,4,4\right)\end{aligned}
$$

For $0\le t\le1$, the velocity and speed are

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r^{\prime}(t)&=\left(-2,3,3\right) \\  \|\mathbf r^{\prime}(t)\|&=\sqrt{(-2)^2+(3)^2+(3)^2} \\  &=\sqrt{22}\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute all three coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf r(t))&=(3 - 2 t)(3 t + 1)^2 \\  &=- 18 t^{3} + 15 t^{2} + 16 t + 3\end{aligned}
$$

Integrate the expanded polynomial and subtract the endpoint values:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C f\,\mathrm{d}s&=\sqrt{22}{\int }_{0}^{1}(- 18 t^{3} + 15 t^{2} + 16 t + 3)\,\text{d}t \\  &=\sqrt{22}\left[- \frac{9 t^{4}}{2} + 5 t^{3} + 8 t^{2} + 3 t\right]_0^1 \\  &=\sqrt{22}\left(\left(\frac{23}{2}\right)-(0)\right) \\  &=\frac{23 \sqrt{22}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$
